title: JetBrains Details Its First Steps to Bring Rapidly Growing AI Spend Under Control
gist: JetBrains' development-related AI spend rose roughly tenfold in six months, with most developers using three to five AI tools per month and token consumption inflecting from January 2026 alongside Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6. Rather than standardizing on one or two vendors, JetBrains built Central CLI as a routing chokepoint so tool choice stays open while credits, limits, and accounting sit underneath — a deliberate contrast to Accenture's usage appeals and Uber's monthly caps after burning an annual AI budget in four months.

insights.claim: JetBrains' development-related AI spending increased roughly tenfold in six months, triggering the company's move to centralize AI usage.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: A 10x six-month ramp at a sophisticated tooling vendor is a demand datapoint for model-provider revenue and a warning that enterprise AI budgets are being set an order of magnitude too low.
insights.quote: development-related spending increased roughly tenfold in six months
insights.locator: JetBrains has described how it began centralizing

insights.claim: Token consumption at JetBrains began rising sharply from January 2026, attributed to the arrival of increasingly capable frontier models including Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Model capability, not headcount or seat growth, is the stated driver of token volume — capability releases should be modeled as step-changes in provider revenue, not gradual ramps.
insights.quote: token consumption began rising sharply from January 2026 alongside the arrival of increasingly capable frontier models including Claude Opus 4.5 and 4.6
insights.locator: The change came as AI usage accelerated

insights.claim: Most JetBrains developers were using between three and five AI tools each month, meaning per-developer AI cost is spread across multiple vendor relationships rather than concentrated in one.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Multi-tool-per-developer is the base case, which caps any single coding-assistant vendor's wallet share and makes seat-based ARR estimates unreliable.
insights.locator: The change came as AI usage accelerated

insights.claim: JetBrains initially spent four days manually collecting usage and expense data into spreadsheets just to produce a one-time snapshot of AI spend across providers and tools.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Four days of manual work for a single snapshot quantifies the tooling gap AI FinOps vendors are selling into.
insights.locator: That diversity made understanding the bill

insights.claim: Dashboards built on provider APIs gave continuously updated current and forecasted expenditure views, but provided no convenient way to intervene because requests still went directly from individual tools to their providers.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Observability-only AI cost tools are structurally incomplete — the value accrues to whoever sits in the request path, not whoever reports on it.
insights.quote: The dashboards could show where spending was occurring, but requests still went directly from individual tools to their respective providers.
insights.locator: Visibility, however, did not provide a convenient way

themes.theme: Central CLI as the routing chokepoint

insights.claim: JetBrains expanded a wrapper originally built by a single developer into Central CLI, a common way to invoke both its own and third-party AI tools with requests routed through the company's existing AI platform.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: The winning internal AI-governance pattern is a CLI proxy layer, not procurement policy — a template other enterprises will copy and a category vendors will productize.
insights.locator: The next step emerged from an internal tool

insights.claim: Routing through Central CLI changed the platform's role from observing AI spend after the fact to participating in the traffic that generates it, creating a shared control point between developers and model providers.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: An in-path control point is where enforcement, caching, model substitution and rate limiting all become possible — the strategic layer to own in enterprise AI stacks.
insights.quote: That changed the role of the platform from observing AI spend after the fact to participating in the traffic generating it.
insights.locator: That changed the role of the platform

insights.claim: With Central CLI in place, JetBrains can apply its existing AI-credit system to third-party tools and managers can view spending and configure limits for individual developers, teams, or larger organizational groups.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Internal credit systems extending over third-party tools effectively re-intermediate the vendor relationship — third-party AI tools become fungible line items rather than owned budgets.
insights.locator: That changed the role of the platform

insights.claim: More than 1,000 developers adopted Central CLI within weeks, indicating voluntary uptake of a governance layer rather than mandated migration.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Fast voluntary adoption suggests governance layers can be shipped as developer conveniences — the lowest-friction path to enterprise AI cost control.
insights.locator: More than 1,000 developers adopted Central CLI

themes.theme: Refusing to standardize on one or two tools

insights.claim: JetBrains deliberately rejected the common approach of sharply reducing available tools, arguing the pace of market change makes it impossible to know which tool will be best for a given task even a few months later.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: If sophisticated buyers treat AI tool choice as too volatile to standardize, multi-year enterprise lock-in deals for coding assistants will be harder to close and churn assumptions should be raised.
insights.quote: argued that the pace of change in the market makes it difficult to know which tool will be best for a given task even a few months later
insights.locator: The company deliberately avoided solving the problem

insights.claim: Centralizing the access layer separates two previously entangled concerns: developers keep choosing among supported tools while accounting, access management and spending controls sit underneath them.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: A reusable model for any fast-moving vendor category — govern the substrate, not the selection — and a direct argument against consolidation-driven procurement.
insights.locator: Centralizing the access layer allows those two concerns

insights.claim: JetBrains notes other organizations have standardized on one or two AI products, positioning its own approach as an explicit divergence from that emerging industry norm.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Two competing enterprise AI procurement doctrines are now visible; which one wins determines whether the coding-assistant market concentrates or stays fragmented.
insights.locator: The company deliberately avoided solving the problem

themes.theme: Unresolved gaps and the wider FinOps shift

insights.claim: Central CLI does not yet cover every source of AI expenditure — some terminal-based agents and personal subscriptions remain outside the managed path.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Shadow AI spend via personal subscriptions persists even at companies actively centralizing, meaning reported enterprise AI budgets understate true consumption.
insights.locator: More than 1,000 developers adopted Central CLI

insights.claim: JetBrains is still working out policies for distributing AI budgets fairly between different users and teams, an unsolved allocation problem that the technical control layer does not answer.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Fair-share allocation is the next bottleneck after metering — an open product gap for anyone building enterprise AI cost governance.
insights.locator: More than 1,000 developers adopted Central CLI

insights.claim: The FinOps Foundation has described generative AI as a growing part of the FinOps remit and recommends centralized approaches to tracking AI usage and costs.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: GenAI formally entering the FinOps discipline creates a new budget line and buying center that cloud-cost vendors will race to occupy.
insights.locator: The wider cost-management problem is becoming

insights.claim: Other large organizations have responded to rising AI consumption with restriction rather than infrastructure: Accenture asked employees to curb unnecessary AI use, and Uber introduced monthly limits after exhausting an annual AI budget within four months.
insights.speaker: Matt Foster
insights.so_what: Uber burning a full-year AI budget in four months is the sharpest available datapoint on enterprise AI cost overrun — expect budget resets and hard caps to become a recurring earnings-season theme.
insights.quote: Uber introduced monthly limits after exhausting an annual AI budget within four months
insights.locator: Other organizations have responded more directly
